utterances.text: I don't know who was issuing orders to Jokic at the time. What you're asking me is something that is the subject matter of the theory of command that is being taught at military academies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's actually a very practical matter in this Tribunal and that there are a number of orders in evidence which General Strugar issued to Admiral Jokic and to the 472nd. Have you ever seen any such order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that Jokic was not subordinated to Strugar, that is based upon an assumption, not on anything you have actually seen in writing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is your suggestion, sir, not mine. I was unable to see anything of the sort at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any basis to say Jokic was not subordinated to Strugar other than your own assumption?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not like to make any theories about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate, Mr. Re, that the Tribunal -- the Chamber is happy for you to move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware whether or not the 472nd Battalion belonged to the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, without the 3rd Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any orders in writing in relation to the attack on Srdj on the morning of the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any, nor would an officer of my rank at the time be the person who -- to whom such things would be shown to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been involved, haven't you, in putting into effect cease-fires by implementing orders and ordering your own troops to come back to base or not to fire after a certain time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did honour the cease-fire, and I as a company commander had the obligation to implement my task related to the cease-fire in my unit. This task was assigned to me by the battalion commander. When you are talking about a cease-fire, I'm not sure what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The implementation of a cease-fire, in practical terms, can take many hours from the time the agreement is made to the time it is communicated down to the last person on the ground.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you made aware --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Maybe yes, maybe no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you made aware when you attended the briefing on the 5th of December that cease-fire negotiations at the highest level were taking place or had taken place on that very day in Dubrovnik, in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't aware that a cease-fire was supposed to take effect as from midday on the 6th of December? No one told you that at the briefing on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was an attack on Srdj a mere six hours before a cease-fire were to be implemented would in all probability destroy the cease-fire, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that things turned out the way they did. I was not aware of this cease-fire at such a high level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An assault upon Srdj a mere six hours before a cease-fire was due to be implemented would destroy the chance of a cease-fire coming into effect, wouldn't it? Because both sides would start fighting again.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said a moment ago that it was Kovacevic who informed you about the cease-fire. When was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention any cease-fire, nor that I was told anything by Vladimir Kovacevic. You were asking me about a possibility. A possibility can exist but needn't necessarily exist. In reality, this was not so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A cease-fire came into effect, I think on the 7th of December. You were involved in implementing the cease-fire as a company commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat the date. I think you said the 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. The agreement was signed on the 7th. You were a company commander in charge of a number of troops. When did you find out about the cease-fire or the implementation of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly the date, but probably after this unfortunate attack on Srdj and probably following the talks at this high state level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who informed you that a cease-fire was coming into effect and that you were to take all appropriate measures to implement and honour the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the attack it was probably the battalion command, because I received orders slowly by the -- by the battalion commander. One would not be able to circumvent any military level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you received those orders at a briefing or whether it was communicated to you by some other means such as radio or telephone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unable to have a radio at the time as there was no electricity. Therefore, whatever you could hear over the radio was one thing, and a soldier acts differently. I cannot take my decisions based on what I hear over the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you then, sir -- by that are you saying that Kovacevic gave you those orders directly, either by coming to see you or by you going to see him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object because my colleague is deliberately creating confusion here because when he asked the witness about a radio, he did not specify what sort of a radio he had in mind, and could this please be cleared up. I don't want to say anything else because I wish to abide by the instruction you gave me the other day, but he should specify the radio he has in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't find the question confusing, but it may be worthwhile, Mr. Re, clarifying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stojanovic. All I'm just trying to find out is where were you or how were you told about the cease-fire? Was it Mr. Kovacevic who told you? Was it in his forward command post? Did he come and see you? Did you come and see him? Did you communicate by radio of any sort or telephone or by written order? How was it done? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this sort of thing one wouldn't use a radio or a telephone line or anything of the sort, but what was required was the immediate contact with the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Direct contact, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you now remember how you received the orders in relation to the cease-fire? If you don't remember, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. A lot of time has elapsed since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke earlier about the briefing on the 5th of December IN which Captain Kovacevic told you about the attack on Srdj, planned the attack on Srdj the next day. Did he tell you it would be permissible to fire on the Old Town in some circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you a moment ago that there were never any plans of engaging any targets in Dubrovnik. I told you that we were told that we would receive fire support and that 130-millimetre cannons would be engaged solely against those targets that proved to be devastating, fatal for our troops. And when I say "fatal," I mean that constitute direct threat to the lives of our troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before I started asking you questions, the very last answer you gave to Mr. Petrovic you referred to Captain Kovacevic's briefing, and you said something that sounded like it may be permissible to fire upon targets in the Old Town. In case we misunderstood what you said, what did Captain Kovacevic tell you about when it would be permissible to fire upon the Old Town or targets within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, only in case there was a target which was firing upon our troops to such an extent that we would sustain casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What weapons did Captain Kovacevic tell you you could use in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, he wasn't required to tell us what arms to use. The battalion within its establishment, and speaking specifically of my company, I said I had 7.62 rifles, sniper rifles, machine-guns. So the weaponry that I disposed of within my unit would not permit me to really threaten or endanger anyone in Dubrovnik. Those were infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The briefing was attended by all the units under his command, wasn't it, including the anti-armour unit and the mortar unit as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the anti-armour company and the commander of the 120-millimetre mortar company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What instructions did Captain Kovacevic issue to those commanders about when they could fire on the Old Town and what sort of weapons they could use to fire on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is certainly interesting to you is, first of all, that the 120-millimetre mortar company provides support by firing upon the Srdj feature. The same task was the one had by the other company, by the anti-armour company, that should fire at those targets endangering the action, whereas the action itself is carried out by 130-millimetre guns. And this is something that our unit didn't have. These were the -- these were the weapons that our superior command disposed of. The task itself was very clear: The task was only to capture the Srdj feature, which was above the positions where my unit was deployed. And in capturing the Srdj feature, we were supposed to prevent the constant provocations by the Croatian army that was deployed in the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the 120-millimetre mortar company located on the morning of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the rear I think it was in the Uskoplje area, but I can't quite put my finger on the specific feature or its name. At any rate, as for the firing position, it could have fired on the Srdj feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was firing on that day, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to provide firing support for our attack on the Srdj feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was subordinated directly to Kovacevic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of its establishment, it was within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what orders did you hear him issuing to the mortar company on the morning of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, to fire on the Srdj feature, to carry out firing preparation for the attack, and later to provide support for the taking of the Srdj feature by different kinds of firing. For a unit like that, that should be a simple enough task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, of the Old Town of Dubrovnik being shelled in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which month are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October and November 1991. Were you aware of the Old Town being shelled by the JNA in either of those two months?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And there was no shelling. In October I was there the whole time, as I said. For some time in November I was at home for sick leave, but I certainly would have seen operations like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would have been aware had the Old Town been shelled in either October or November 1991. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I would have been aware? Well, the positions are in fact so close that you can see it. It wasn't anyone's objective to use higher calibre weapons to fire on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, you told the Trial Chamber earlier that you had two T-55 tanks within your company. Were those two tanks directly under your control on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order them to fire on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the tanks, the way it was deployed, was in no position to open fire since it was positioned on the left flank. And the other tank was used for support to the assault group led by Lieutenant Pesic. It could only have fired on the Srdj feature, because in order to prepare all the elements for tank firing and targeting by tank, I had no conditions in place to fire on Dubrovnik, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this tank, the one that could fire? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said -- you mentioned the one that could fire. Well, I'm not sure what fire you have in mind. What I said was that one tank was in the area of the houses at Bosanka, and according to some principles of use, that tank could not be used to target Dubrovnik. The other tank was moving along the asphalt road towards the Srdj feature, and it could have fired on the Srdj feature. Still, in order to use a tank to fire, you need to prepare all the necessary elements. The lay of the land, the sort of terrain that was there, did not allow for this. There was no even theoretical possibility to target Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order the tank to fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Srdj feature?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anywhere.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't order the tank to fire just anywhere. My assessment of the situation is that one tank could open fire on the Srdj feature, and that wasn't just anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I'm asking you is did you actually order the tank to fire. Did you or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's difficult to remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you order the tank to fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time when I was under fire and when I was sustaining casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time was that? I mean, how long after the attack began? Half an hour, hour, 15 minutes, two hours, three hours, four hours?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the attack began, not after. What do you mean how long before the attack? The tank never fired before the attack began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually said after, but how long after the attack did you order the tank to fire? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular tank was providing support for the assault group coming in. Therefore, as the assault group was coming in, but later there are no conditions any longer for firing, because you can't fire a tank randomly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you for a time. Approximately what time in the morning did you order the tank to fire? Was it 6.00 a.m., 6.15, 6.30, 7.00, earlier or later? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer the question, not even roughly speaking. It's been 13 or 14 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a record kept of how many times a tank fires, how many rounds it uses? Is that recorded anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That tank which you've just described was, of course, capable of firing on Dubrovnik and the Old Town, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Old Town of Dubrovnik was within firing range of that tank, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, it's about the sort of terrain that was there. From my position, I couldn't see Dubrovnik with the naked eye. Therefore, I was in no position to plan any firing using that tank against Dubrovnik or the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tank was in a position where it could have been moved to fire on Dubrovnik, wasn't it, by moving through the terrain?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It could not be moved, and no firing on Dubrovnik had been envisaged. What was said is that there should be support by 130-millimetre guns. For that sort of assignment, that would have been quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying it was the 130-millimetre gun which was supposed to fire on the Old Town of Dubrovnik, if needed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I said is that the 130-millimetre guns were supposed to neutralise such targets as were firing at our men with fatal consequences. As for the targets, I think you need to go and ask the commanders of those specific units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your tank, the tank under your command, firing at a time when Croatian forces in the Dubrovnik area were firing at the JNA in the Srdj area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say now how long the firing between your tank, on the one hand, and the firing from the Croatian forces went on for?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order your tank to fire against any Croatian forces that were firing from the Dubrovnik region at the JNA troops on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was being fired at by mortars from Dubrovnik. I was in no position to neutralise such targets because the terrain would not have allowed it. That is the lay of the land. I would not have been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's coming, Mr. Stojanovic, the Old Town of Dubrovnik is two and a half -- sorry, about 2.3 kilometres in a direct line from Zarkovica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that distance, with the naked eye you could make out vehicles and possibly the shapes of people, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me now -- I said before that from Zarkovica I could see and I did indeed see movements by Croatian soldiers carrying long barrels. So I'm not sure what this question is about. I'm not sure I understand you fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just have a look at Exhibit P16, which is the photograph which is on the screen to your right. It should also be on the computer. Now, that's a photograph taken from Zarkovica. That is the very edge of Zarkovica looking directly towards the Old Town, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that photograph represents the view, a person standing on the very edge of Zarkovica where the gravel is of the Old Town, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at that photograph, even though it's slightly unclear, even if it were clearer, you would not be able to make out people carrying long-barrelled weapons with the naked eye, would you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That's not how it was, sir. From Zarkovica you could see people moving about in the Old Town, in addition to which we soldiers had certain tools that we could use, and we could see very clearly and be certain exactly who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zarkovica is even further back from where that photograph is taken, isn't it? This photograph is at the very edge, the edge of the cliff, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this photograph was taken from, sir. What I'm telling you is what I can see from Zarkovica, what one can see from Zarkovica and what I could indeed see from Zarkovica at the time. Now to theorise where a certain photograph has been taken from, I don't think that's in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You certainly don't have photographs of these troops moving around the Old Town, do you? No one took any photographs of them, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the requisite equipment in my company to pursue those photographic activities, sir. Being a soldier, it would have been sufficient for me to have a look in order for me to see what I saw, and what I saw is what I've already told you. I mean, who in their right state of mind would pursue photographic matters in the middle of a war, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your understanding of Captain Kovacevic's orders about military activity within the Old Town that you could fire upon, use the weapons on the 6th of December to fire upon people or soldiers with long-barrelled weapons, rifles, in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was given the task to take the Srdj feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe it's the way I asked it. When I said "you," I meant the group that he was briefing, that is all his subordinate company commanders. Was it your understanding of his orders that he was permitting fire upon soldiers with long-barrelled arms in the Old Town on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, those people carrying long-barrelled weapons could not attack us, but they did eventually use a mortar to attack us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I was asking you about Captain Kovacevic's orders on the 5th of December. Was it your understanding that his orders to the group, all the subordinate commanders, allowed or permitted firing by whatever means upon people with long-barrelled weapons in the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my understanding was what the task was in relation to my own unit, and that was the main thing for me. From my position, I could not possibly target anyone like you suggest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first contacted by the Defence of General Strugar, that is to give a statement to them or to speak to them about what happened? Was it this year, last year, the year before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long ago; this month, last month, months ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a month ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you give a statement, that is did you put something in writing to the Defence, that is Mr. Petrovic or Mr. Rodic, or a legal assistant or an investigator?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take notes when you spoke to them? Sorry, who did you speak to; was it Mr. Petrovic or Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he take notes of what you said to him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody has a notepad in front of him. It's not for me to look at that kind of thing. It is for me to give answers to the best of my knowledge and to the degree to which I can assist. You'll have to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was about a month ago. Did he come and see you wherever you live in that area, or did you go to his office?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have approval of the General Staff to the effect that I can make statements. So these preparations take place for participation in this defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying he saw you in the army barracks, in Belgrade or somewhere like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't work in Belgrade. He didn't come to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Petrovic when he saw you, you saw him about a month ago, about you seeing Croatian soldiers with long-barrelled weapons in Zarkovica? Did you tell him that then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I say what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Petrovic, when you spoke to him about a month ago at some unnamed destination -- or location, about your seeing from Zarkovica, with the naked eye, Croatian soldiers moving around the Old Town carrying long-barrelled weapons? Did you tell him that when you saw him about a month ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, questions were put to me, and as for what I saw, I said that I saw this from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to be quite clear, you told Mr. Petrovic a month ago, did you, that you saw those soldiers, with your naked eye, in Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with an artillery compass, if you know what that is. That is used for looking through it, and you can see exactly what movements are made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told Mr. Petrovic something different to what you've told the Trial Chamber today, and that is that you saw it with your naked eye. Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say anything different today or then. I said that it could be seen with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever make any reports to anyone, that is put in writing what you claim you saw in the Old Town, that is the soldiers moving around?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever tell anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody could see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. Did you yourself, Mr. Stojanovic, ever tell anyone about it, tell a commander, a superior officer about what you'd seen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw was the same thing that my battalion commander, Vlado Kovacevic, saw from Zarkovica too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just two questions. Re-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were asked about this tank, tell us, please, what was the function of this tank within the planned action of attacking Srdj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The function of this tank was to support the attack group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could this tank open fire at the feature of Srdj at the time when your assault group was there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. A mortar couldn't let alone a tank when the unit was at that feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the tank that was within your unit could not open fire at the positions in the town of Dubrovnik because of the characteristics of the terrain. What are these characteristics of the terrain which make it impossible to open fire from that tank at targets in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said, Mr. Petrovic, that these geographic characteristics of the terrain are such that if I were to prepare any kind of firing, I would have to go at least 300 metres further down in order to be able to prepare any kind of fire. So that would not be tactically justified and I could not do that. So my units, my company could not open fire due to the terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At which altitude was the tank, and at which altitude is the town of Dubrovnik, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can have a look. The tank was at the altitude of the village of Bosanka, and Dubrovnik is further down, as far as altitude is concerned. I cannot tell you anything off-the-cuff now because I don't have a map in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, did Kovacevic issue any kind of orders regarding an attack on the Old Town or opening fire at the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the only objective of your action on the 6th of December to take the feature of Srdj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only objective was to take the feature of Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My objection was on the basis of leading, but the question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colonel Stojanovic, thank you very much for your attendance. You are free to go now. I'm sure you will be pleased to get away and ease your back again. So thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of the slightly shorter period due to the last witness's back condition, we are a little out of anticipated time. We had planned to have a break for approximately an hour for lunch today. Would it be convenient to have that break now rather than much later? I think that would suit everybody and even up the day. So we will resume at 1.30 and have the new witness then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you please stand and read the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would kindly ask you to give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: My name is Nemanja Kurdulija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kurdulija, could you please tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I was born on the 7th of January, 1957, in the village of Korita, Bileca municipality, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I am an officer in the army of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What school did you finish?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Secondary maritime school in Kotor, naval technical military academy in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any speciality?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been in the army service?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Since 10th September, 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you with your service in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I was a member of the 9th Naval Sector, and my unit was the 69th naval and technical rocket base, headquartered on Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 were any combat operations taking place while you were at Prevlaka?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Not at Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when combat operations commenced in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps in which month?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: It was in late September of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay the whole time with the 69th naval technical rocket base at Prevlaka?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you transferred from that position?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I was transferred to the post of the commander, town commander of Cavtat upon orders from the command of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone issue this kind of order to you personally?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The then commander of the 69th unit, Lieutenant Colonel Ukropina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you came to the town command of Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: It was on the 19th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what was the situation in the town of Cavtat when you arrived there? Were there local residents in the place?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were local residents, and I estimate there were about 6.000 of them. The local residents were not only from Cavtat itself but from the villages in Konavle. They were accommodated in hotels and some of them in private houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation concerning water and energy supply at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: The electric power supply was cut off due to combat operations between JNA units and paramilitary Croatian units. The same situation was concerning water supply. Therefore, there was neither electric power nor water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage later to provide energy and water for Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Very soon thereafter, within seven or eight days, with the assistance of the superior command and professionals from Herceg Novi and Trebinje municipalities, we managed to fully restore the power and water supplies for Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your task, among other things, to provide food for the local population?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, but not only that. Everything that was conducive and in the interests of normalisation of life in the town. In all these areas, the command took initiatives and helped bring the life to normal. Within that context, some of the most needed staples, products just like flour or gas for home cooking were provided from Herceg Novi and people were able to be provided with these bare necessities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any manpower subordinated to you and that you were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a platoon of soldiers and three or four officers and junior officers who were in my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have military police in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the military policemen under your command as well?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: They had their officers who commanded them, platoon and company commanders, and they were directly subordinated to the command of the military police battalion and the security organs from the command of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a local council in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I'd rather say that we established a local council there, if you allow me to explain, because before our command was established, they had had a Crisis Staff which we naturally could not accept as such. In other words, the local council was established and made up of people who had held certain positions in Cavtat and who were familiar with the town itself and the area in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you cooperate with this local council in organising life in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was the local population allowed to leave Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, they were. It was made possible for them to do so immediately after our command was set up. That primarily referred to those who wanted to go and see their houses, their estates in the villages in Konavle wherefrom their forces had evacuated them and brought them to Cavtat. In addition to that, everyone who wished to do so, for instance to visit their relatives or to procure food and similar goods, were allowed to leave to the neighbouring municipalities of Herceg Novi, Kotor, Tivat, Trebinje, and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your command post headquartered?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: In the Tiha Bay offices of Atlas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a tourist or travel agency?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when your command was housed on the premises of the Atlas travel agency?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Approximately until mid December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those offices where the town command was, what facilities, communications facilities you had?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I had only one wire telephone which was connected with our line according to the scheme of lines that were applicable at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that that was an army telephone?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively for the use by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the premises of the command in Cavtat, did you have radio relay devices?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any radio or radio relay devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps have portable radio stations?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, we didn't have portable radio stations either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, by this telephone, this wire connection as you explained, were you able to establish communications with units of the naval military sector in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: We were able to do so, that means to establish telephone communications, but indirectly, with basic units that were at the time part of the sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the forward command post was of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was, for a certain period of time, within the compound of the Cilipi airport and later in the area of Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- could you establish telephone communication with the forward command post in Kupari from Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your command post in Cavtat, could you use this army telephone to establish communications with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, but through the exchange in Kumbor, which means indirectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be more specific and explain, how do you establish a connection with Belgrade in an indirect manner?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I would use my telephone to give a code, my code, and I requested to be connected to a certain number. For instance, in the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the same procedure was applied vice versa?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: The communication existed with our exchange in Kumbor. So my answer to your question is yes, regardless of the fact that the men from Kumbor could maybe convey a message or an order or anything that related to us and that was coming from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kurdulija, I would like to hear from you, was it possible for someone from Belgrade to use this military line and contact you in the town command of Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1991, were you at the town command of Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone come to your command on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Admiral Jokic came to see me on that day in my command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that an announced visit?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at what time Admiral Jokic came to see you in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was between 9.30 [Realtime transcript read in error "9.10"] and 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, for how long did the admiral stay at your command post in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Please, before I answer let me correct a mistake. I said between 9.30 and 10.00, and I see on the screen that it says 9.10 and 10.00. So I would like this to be corrected. And could you please now repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Do you remember, for how long did Admiral Jokic stay at the command post in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that it all happened 13 years ago, as far as I can remember now, according to my estimate, he stayed between one and a half and two hours at the command post in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Admiral Jokic came to your command, did he ask you anything?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He asked me the usual questions relating to the operation of my command, and he was generally interested in the situation in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report to him on the situation at your command?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I presented the details to him concerning our work and the general -- the situation in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that, did Admiral Jokic request anything else from you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: On that day, after some time, he requested me to get in touch with the forward command post that was at the time in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he do that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: He requested that because he wanted some officers to report to him who had been his closest associates at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did he refer specifically to?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I remember that he wanted to talk to Colonel Gavro Kovacevic and that he wanted the Warship Captain Milan Zec to come to Cavtat, where he was, in order to have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do about these requests of Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: In fact, on that occasion I only got in touch with the forward command post. I can't remember who was the duty operations officer at the forward command post, and Admiral Jokic issued these tasks over the phone to the officer who answered the call at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Admiral Jokic was at the command post in Cavtat, apart from this conversation, did he talk to anyone else over your phone?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: He made one or two more telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long these telephone conversations lasted?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Those were not long telephone conversations as far as I can remember. They each lasted a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, who did he talk to?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I don't remember who he talked with, nor can I remember which particular orders he gave during those conversations, because those conversations were short, and while he was there and with his approval I discharged my regular daily duties from the purview of the responsibilities of the town command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Admiral Jokic was there in the offices of the town command of Cavtat, did you ever leave the office?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, I never left the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any calls over this phone while Admiral Jokic was there with you in the office?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving any calls at that time. The officers who were with me at the command and the platoon that I mentioned earlier, I assigned tasks to them directly, not over the phone. So I don't think it was necessary that any of my colleagues from the command or soldiers called me on the phone during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at all the subject and the content of the conversations that Admiral Jokic conducted over your phone?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the content because I believed those to be the usual methods of communications between the commander of the 9th VPS and his officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this one and a half to two hours that you said that Admiral Jokic had spent at your command, apart from these telephone conversations that you've -- that you mentioned that he had made, was your telephone line free?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: The telephone line was free, yes. I don't recall there having been any discontinuations in the line that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Admiral Jokic was at the command post in Cavtat in your office, did you know what the purpose was of his visit that wasn't announced?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I didn't know because it was customary for him to simply show up unannounced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until that day, the 6th of December, and keeping in mind the time -- the date when you entered your duty as the head of the Cavtat town command, did he ever show up earlier on?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes. He was there two times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear any combat activities on that day from Cavtat from the offices you were in? Could you hear any military activities?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, you could, but we didn't know what was going on that day because it was quite normal for sporadic activities to take place from the time I entered my post up until the 6th of December, the date you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, from your command post could one see Zarkovica, Mokosica, and other places where the 9th VPS units were deployed?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: You mean whether you could reach them by telephone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, normal wire telephone line.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Over the telephone line that we talked about, one could convey orders to them through their basic units. One could also receive a message as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, while Admiral Jokic was in the command of the town of Cavtat, was there anyone else coming to the command?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: The admiral arrived alone with, naturally, the driver who did not accompany him to the command headquarters but remained in the car. Later on, while he was still there, the Warship Captain Milan Zec also arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when it was during his stay in your command post that Warship Captain Milan Zec came?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was within the last half hour of his stay there, and I'm talking about the admiral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the two of them do at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: They talked, and they, however, asked me to leave the room while they were talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore you are not aware of the subject matter of their conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What course did the visit of Admiral Jokic and Captain Milan Zec take at your command post following their talks?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Upon the completion of their talks, they left the command post individually, at different times, and I was not able to see where they went since the position of the agency premises was such as would not allow us to see which direction they took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you had stayed in Cavtat for a while and the 9th VPS units were deployed there, can you tell us what the distance is between Cavtat and Kupari, and how long does it take for you if you're driving in a vehicle to reach Kupari from Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: In my estimate, ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, could you tell me what the distance between Cavtat and Cilipi is? How long does it take you to drive there in a car?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have finished my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. We are asked to observe a period of silence in memory of Sir Richard May, whose funeral is taking place at this time. We will do that now. Thank you very much. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kurdulija.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still serving in the army of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your rank is colonel?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As such I will refer to you as "Colonel." Colonel Kurdulija, now, in examination-in-chief you referred to taking certain steps in Cavtat with the assistance of the superior command. Which formation or which command did you mean when you referred to the words "superior command"? Was it the 2nd Operational Group that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I primarily referred to the command of the 9th Naval Military Sector and also then the 2nd Operational Strategic Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Pipovic is?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Pipovic, if it's him you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm referring to Colonel Pipovic. And wasn't he an officer directly subordinated to General Strugar who was also assigned to Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Pipovic was the assistant to General Strugar for civilian affairs, that is for the civilian sector, and he was stationed in Sutorina, near Igalo. So your information is not correct. Furthermore, Colonel Pipovic was my superior but only until mid-December 1991 when he, together with his command, arrived in the area and started his operation. He was second in my command, and I'm referring to the area around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at some stage he did act as your superior?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes, but as my second superior, because he had two subordinated commands. One was in Cavtat and was in charge of the area from Debeli Brijeg-Sutorina to Mokosica. And this command was in Cavtat, whereas Colonel Radojevic was in charge of the command and they were my immediate superiors until mid-December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned that on 6th December Admiral Jokic arrived at Cavtat, and could you not exactly remember the time, but you thought it was sometime between - correct me if I'm wrong - I think you said 9.30 and 10.00. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said he probably remained for about -- till about approximately 1.30 -- or I'm sorry, one and a half hours to two hours. So that would place him in Cavtat till about 12.00, approximately. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: The first part you mentioned, 1.30, that's not correct. In -- as far as I remember, he stayed there for about one and a half hours to two hours, which could make it then up to midday, but this first part that I can read from my -- on my screen, until about approximately 1.30, that's not correct. It should be deleted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kurdulija, I made a mistake there and you will see in the transcript that I apologise and go on to correct myself by saying one and a half hours to two hours. It was a mistake I made when I said 1.30. So you do agree that would place Admiral Jokic in Cavtat around noon?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: That's what I said. Now, whether he remained there until noon, 12.00 noon or a minute earlier, a minute later, I can't state with precision, but I did say that he stayed there for about one and a half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he left Cavtat and went to Cilipi to take a helicopter to Podgorica. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I never asked my superiors where they were headed. He left Cavtat. Now, where he went, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Admiral Jokic was at Cavtat, did he assign you any tasks? Did he dictate any faxes to be sent off or did he hand over any messages to be given to Captain Zec or any messages to be conveyed to Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No. Whatever tasks he issued were issued there on the spot. I've already said so. He asked me to get in touch with the forward command post at Kupari, and he himself issued the tasks. So I did not receive any tasks, not even with regard to the organisation of life and work in the town, which used to be the practice of him issuing such tasks earlier on when he would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he dictate any letters or telegrams to you to be handed over to Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No. There was no need for him to because he personally talked to Captain Zec in my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that he used the telephone. Now, where exactly is the telephone located in your command post?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: It was located in the office where I would stay. Yes, there in the office where I would stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that while Admiral Jokic was present at Cavtat, you, with his permission, attended to your other general tasks. Now, what are your general or daily general tasks that you attended to on that day? You don't have to go into detail, but a general description would do.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: First of all, the officers and the platoon commander who was subordinated to me reported to me and provided me with the proposal for the plan of what had to be done in the course of that day. And we're talking about the afternoon hours. And he allowed me to receive the commander in this particular room. And while I was approving the plan to this commander, and now it's not important whether the plan concerned the touring of these civilians who were there in Konavle, who were trying to visit there homes, because not all of them had vehicles, or whether it concerned something else, meanwhile the admiral had his own documents he had to attend to, and I was there on the spot giving my approval to this commander, and the same was done with my duty officer at the command, the same was done with my associate administrator who was in charge of my office correspondence. To put it briefly, whatever contacts I had to make, I made them in the same room where the -- where he was up until he left, that is up until he actually started talking to Captain Zec when I left the room. If you're interested in any other details concerning my work, I would kindly ask you to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you stressing the fact that you were present in the room right through when I asked you that? Were you instructed to testify to such effect by anybody? Because I never asked you where you were right through. I only asked you what your general tasks were. Why are you stressing that fact?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Nobody instructed me to that effect. I've emphasised this fact because I'm kind of expecting the logical drift of your questions, future questions. How would you have known if you had not been there? And it was from this logic that I started from. And this room where we were, the premises where we were were quite small. There were two rooms; one duty officer's room and my room. This was simply for the civilians to come to ask, put forward the different requests to my officers. There was a desk there to that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So what you're saying is that you spoke to your other officers, gave them instructions, did everything in the presence of their commander who was also there taking telephone calls. That is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No. Please do not put the words in my mouth, because during his stay there he made these one or two telephone calls, and he did not talk all the while. He was there. He had certain documents that he had to attend to - I don't wish to repeat myself - and he allowed me to do whatever I needed to do with my officers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware on the 6th that there was a cease-fire agreement that was to be signed in Cavtat that day at 12.00?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. May I just note that any negotiations that were conducted were beyond my purview, and I did not know when they were taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that there were negotiations conducted on the 5th in Cavtat, between Admiral Jokic, your commander, and three ministers of the Croatian side? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So being the commander of Cavtat, you did not know that there were negotiations being conducted between your commander and the Croatian party on a comprehensive cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: You should not be surprised at that, at the fact that I did not know. My command was a low-level command. My task was primarily a humanitarian one, to take care of people there in that area, and that once our command arrived there that they could continue living a normal life. The high-level negotiations that were conducted by Admiral Jokic is something I was not supposed to be aware of. I was not interested in that, and therefore I was not informed about it. Admiral Jokic commanded all the units in the sector, and he could enter any area where any unit of ours was in charge and that I or any other unit commander did not even have to know that he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had heard that there was -- or heard the sound of combat activity from Cavtat. At what time -- I beg your pardon. I withdraw that. When Admiral Jokic came to Cavtat, did you inquire from him what the combat activity was all about or did you or Admiral Jokic ever discuss this? Was it natural for you to ask Admiral Jokic what is going on?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Please. You gave a few questions now -- or, rather, you put a few questions now. If it's all right with you, can we move from one question to another? I understand a bit of English myself, and I see these dashes on the transcript, so can we deal with the questions one at a time so that I could give a better answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kurdulija, it's just one question. My question is: Did you discuss with Admiral Jokic when you arrived what was going on, the combat activity? That's just one question.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: No, because my unit was not an operative unit. It was there purely for logistical reasons, and there was no need for me to be afraid for my own officers or NCOs or soldiers because there was no combat activity in Cavtat. I did not ask the admiral out of respect for my superior officer. It is not for me to put questions to him. I was not supposed to ask him questions that did not belong to my own line of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kurdulija, when you mentioned that you had heard some combat activity, can you give us a more detailed description in terms of what you actually meant?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: What I meant was that artillery mortar shells could be heard and sporadic infantry gunfire, gunfire coming from infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that day, the 6th of December, did you have the opportunity of hearing such activities earlier on?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This kind of fire, regardless of whether it's just infantry fire or mortar or artillery fire or both, such fire was heard over the past few days, too, but we were not supposed to receive such reports in Cavtat, so we did not really know whether somebody was shooting for the fun of it or whether it was an exchange of gunfire between JNA units and the Croatian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in that period when you mentioned that Admiral Jokic, before the 6th of December, came two or three other times to your command post, did you ever discuss combat activities?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA KURDULIJA
utterances.text: Never. That was never the subject of our conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain. That's all that your evidence involves. We are grateful for your attendance and your assistance, and you are now free to return to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately at this moment the Defence does not have a witness who is ready to enter the courtroom. We did not think that the examination of Mr. Stojanovic, the company commander who took part in the Srdj activities, would be so short, so we only had this witness prepared for today. However, it is for this reason that my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, left the courtroom earlier, so that the Defence would have three witnesses who would be ready to enter the courtroom tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have witnesses here in The Hague, though?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, can the next one be ready at 3.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could not answer that question before contacting my colleague Mr. Petrovic, because I know that he went to conduct the proofing of that witness with whom he intends to start first thing in the morning tomorrow. The second witness who will be testifying tomorrow in court is due to arrive this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we can simply afford to wait until tomorrow. Clearly the witness is coming here with an appreciation on the part of the Defence of the evidence that witness will give and the point the witness is to be called for. Detailed proofing may make the evidence a little quicker, but that is all. Is the proofing taking place in the building here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Unfortunately, we do not have the facilities for that. Our witnesses are in two different hotels in completely different parts of town, so we have quite a few technical difficulties in our work too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When will -- where is this witness and Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are at the Sofitel Hotel, near the central railway station in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that witness's name is?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That witness's name is Budimir Pesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's thought he'll be a relatively short witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps not relatively short, but our estimate is that his effective time, including examination in chief and cross-examination, would be between two and two and a half hours. It is for that reason that we have planned to have two more witnesses ready for tomorrow after him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He was noted on the 65 ter as one hour, which is, by the scale of things, a short witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view, Mr. Rodic, that we would adjourn now with a view to resuming at quarter past 3.00. If you could be good enough to arrange for the witness and Mr. Petrovic to be here at that time, we'll continue with the evidence then. That will give 35 minutes, which is more than enough to get in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can make it half past three, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Your Honours adjourn, there's an application I wish to make in respect of the witness before, and I'm sorry I haven't notified my learned friend and all the Chambers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to delay Mr. Rodic at this moment as he has to get word --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. But it could impact on that. It's an application in relation to the previous witness, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There will be an application by the Prosecution to recall him to cross-examine on one specific point. During my cross-examination I, unfortunately, neglected to ask him in relation to the matter of discipline which he raised in his examination-in-chief. His evidence was that discipline was not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I just neglected, and there was a specific document, which is P108, in which the Prosecution case is contained in relation to discipline which I neglected to put to him, as the Prosecution is, of course, required to do under Rule 90 (H) of the Rules. Now, the fact that I haven't done it, put the Trial Chamber and the Defence on notice doesn't mean we abandon in any way that part of the case, but I have an application. The witness is still in The Hague - we've spoken to VMS [sic], and is at one of these hotels - and is potentially recallable if the Trial Chamber is minded to allow me to recall for cross-examination on that point, either today or first thing tomorrow morning. I anticipate if I was given the leave, I wouldn't be more than between five or ten minutes on that specific point. Again, I apologise for what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the application to recall the witness, Mr. Rodic, do you have any submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence opposes this request put forth by the Prosecution, but at any rate, the Defence leaves the ultimate decision in the hands of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will sit again at 3.30. If the previous witness can be here at that time, we will allow him to be recalled. That may take five or ten minutes, all of which will give Mr. Petrovic a little longer in his proofing, but the further witness will follow immediately on the completion of the cross-examination and any re-examination. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one brief point. We have not received any sort of proofing notes, any summary, any changes in this witness, the upcoming witness's testimony, because we were going to get it tonight for tomorrow. Does that mean we're going to go right into cross-examination or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There would seem to be no hope of that. The time will run out before you're reached. So you will have all the small hours of the night to prepare for cross-examination, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're always thinking of you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I gather before we resume with evidence that there is some matter that is to be raised. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. We had requested, if possible, some idea, if the Chamber is in a position to perhaps let us know, of what the final submissions schedule would ultimately be. I know there have been informal discussions among the Defence and us and the legal officers, but we were trying to map out the balance of this month and how August would look, if the Chamber is in a position, and I would have to leave it entirely, of course, in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the immediate expectation is that we will finish the evidence on Friday the 23rd, I think it is, of this month. We will then have a break which will in part coincide with the normal vacation of the Tribunal with an expectation for the parties to have prepared and have filed their final submissions. The initial thought of the Tribunal was that that would take a month. I don't have a diary with me at the moment to pinpoint that date, but it would be somewhere in the vicinity of 23rd of August. There would then be need for a provision for final submissions.
